title: America Is Rationing Cancer Drugs. The FDA Just Called India for Help.
excerpt: Hospitals can fill barely a third of their orders for a critical chemotherapy drug. Now the FDA's India office has turned to Cipla, Zydus and at least two other Indian manufacturers to plug the gap.
body:
In oncology wards across the United States, the math is getting brutal. Hospitals purchasing through Premier, a group-buying organisation that represents roughly 4,200 health systems, have been able to fill just 38 per cent of their orders for ifosfamide — a chemotherapy drug used to treat sarcomas, lymphomas and testicular cancers. Cisplatin, a mainstay for ovarian, testicular and bladder cancers, is running at about two-thirds supply. Doctors in Michigan are already meeting to decide which patients get treated first.

"There are some individuals who will not be able to receive this drug, even if it is the best option for them," said Dr Andrew Shuman, a head and neck cancer surgeon and professor at the University of Michigan. "That puts pharmacists, doctors, patients and families in a horrific situation."

The shortage is not new — it traces to manufacturing disruptions at Baxter International, one of the largest suppliers of injectable chemotherapy drugs — but it has tipped into a crisis that the FDA can no longer manage domestically. On June 18, the agency's India office sent a formal communication to the Indian Drug Manufacturers' Association, asking it to identify manufacturers capable of supplying ifosfamide injection in 1-gram and 3-gram strengths.

## India's pharma giants are already moving

The response from Indian industry has been swift. According to Viranchi Shah, the national spokesperson of the IDMA, four companies are being considered as frontrunners: **Zydus Lifesciences**, **Cipla**, **Alkem Laboratories** and **Aurobindo Pharma's GLS unit** — all of which already manufacture the molecule and hold established positions in the American market.

"The IDMA has informed the Indian government about manufacturers capable of producing the medicine," Shah said. The association's role, he clarified, is limited to identifying capable members and connecting them with the relevant authorities. Commercial discussions are happening directly between the companies and the US side.

The FDA has signalled unusual flexibility. In its communication, the agency said it would consider products approved and marketed in countries other than the United States, and would even evaluate medicines from facilities that are not FDA-registered — provided they have a strong record of regulatory compliance.

## Why India, and why now

India's pharmaceutical infrastructure makes it the obvious call. The country has roughly 10,500 pharmaceutical manufacturing units, including more than 350 facilities registered with the US FDA. It supplies nearly a fifth of the world's generic medicines and ranks third globally by production volume. For injectable oncology drugs specifically, Indian manufacturers have built deep capability after years of supplying both US generics markets and global institutional buyers.

The shortage itself is a reminder of how concentrated — and fragile — the global supply chain for essential cancer medicines has become. These are decades-old drugs, inexpensive to buy but demanding to manufacture in sterile facilities. Low margins have driven multiple producers out of the market over the years, leaving supply dependent on a handful of plants. When one goes down, the pipeline drains fast.

An earlier episode, in 2022-23, made the vulnerability painfully clear. An FDA inspection of an Indian facility run by Intas Pharmaceuticals — which at one point produced half the cisplatin and 20 per cent of the carboplatin used in the United States — uncovered severe quality violations, including freshly torn-up documents that had been doused in acid. The resulting production halt triggered a national chemotherapy shortage.

## The market has noticed

Investors have read the signal clearly. The Nifty Pharma index gained 2.1 per cent for the week, outperforming the broader market as analysts flagged the FDA outreach as a potential export opportunity for Indian drugmakers. Shares of Cipla, Alkem and Zydus rose up to 2.4 per cent in the sessions following the news.

Adding to the momentum, **Lupin** announced on Friday that it had received tentative FDA approval for generic enzalutamide tablets — a treatment for castration-resistant prostate cancer sold under the brand Xtandi by Astellas. Lupin's version covers four strengths, including 120 mg and 160 mg variants not currently available from the originator, potentially expanding dosing options for US oncologists.

The pharma sector has been one of India's strongest market performers in 2026, gaining over 11 per cent year-to-date against a 7.7 per cent decline in the benchmark Nifty 50. The combination of weakening rupee (improving export margins), a defensive rotation away from oil-sensitive sectors, and now direct FDA demand for Indian supply, has made the thesis hard to argue against.

## The diaspora angle

For the roughly 4.8 million Indian Americans in the United States, the story lands at an uncomfortable intersection. Many work in the very health systems managing these shortages — Indian-origin physicians, pharmacists and researchers are disproportionately represented in American oncology. At the same time, the companies being called upon to fill the gap are headquartered in Mumbai, Ahmedabad and Hyderabad.

It is a reminder that India's role in the global health architecture extends well beyond cheap generics. When the world's richest country cannot produce enough of a cancer drug discovered in the 1950s, and turns to India's manufacturing base for emergency supply, the old "pharmacy of the world" label starts to look less like a cliché and more like a structural fact.

The more urgent question is whether the fix arrives in time. Baxter's 3-gram ifosfamide vials are on back order until mid-August at the earliest. The 1-gram vials are on limited allocation. For patients whose treatment windows are measured in weeks, the gap between a formal FDA request and actual shipments landing in American hospitals is not academic — it is the difference between getting treated and being told to wait.
